title: VFDs, Disconnects, and Motor Starters: Who Pays in Your Scope Letter
summary: Electrical or mechanical? VFDs, motor starters, and disconnects live in the grey zone. Here's how GCs close the gap before the sub disputes it in the field.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- VFDs, motor starters, and disconnects sit at the electrical/mechanical boundary. Without a written assignment in the scope letter, both trades will exclude them.
- The most common gap: the mechanical sub installs the equipment, the electrical sub wires it, and nobody owns the disconnect, the starter panel, or the VFD housing.
- This gap is showing up more in data center and healthcare work, where specs run 2,000+ pages and trade boundaries are buried in Division 23 and Division 26.
- Fix it at buyout, not in the field. Write it down, cite the section, and get a confirmation from each trade.
- Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) reads the full project set and flags these cross-trade gaps before bid day.


## The Dispute That Repeats Itself


Ask any estimator who has worked a healthcare or data center project about VFDs. You will hear the same story, told with different numbers and different subs.


The mechanical sub installs the air handling unit. The electrical sub runs power to the panel. Somewhere between those two scopes lives a variable frequency drive, a motor starter, and a disconnect switch. Neither sub included them. Both assumed the other would. The GC absorbs the cost.


This is not a rare edge case. According to Provision's research across 200+ GC interviews, generator field conditioning and MEP equipment boundaries are among the most frequently cited recurring scope gaps on commercial and ICI projects. The dollar amounts are rarely small.


A 2018 PlanGrid and FMI study found that $31.3 billion in U.S. construction rework was tied to miscommunication and bad project data. That figure is from 2018, but the root cause has not changed. Scope boundaries that are never written down produce disputes that repeat across every project.


## Why VFDs, Starters, and Disconnects Are the Problem


These three components sit at the intersection of two trade divisions. That is the problem.


- **Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs):** Control motor speed. They show up in Division 23 (HVAC) and Division 26 (Electrical). The spec may assign supply to one trade and installation to another. It often does not say who provides the disconnect or the conduit from the VFD to the motor.
- **Motor starters:** Start and stop motors. Sometimes integral to the VFD. Sometimes a standalone panel item. Mechanical subs expect them in the electrical scope. Electrical subs assume the mechanical sub is coordinating with the equipment supplier.
- **Disconnects:** Required by code at or near the motor. The spec may show them on the electrical drawings and describe them in the mechanical spec. Without a named trade in your scope letter, neither sub owns them.


The confusion compounds when the equipment supplier for the HVAC unit offers a factory-mounted starter as an option. If nobody confirms whether that option was exercised, the electrical sub prices a standalone starter that is already included in the mechanical sub's equipment quote.


## What Specifications Actually Say (and What They Leave Out)


The spec language rarely resolves this cleanly. Here is what you will typically find:


Component Typical Spec Location What It Usually Says What It Usually Leaves Out


VFD Division 23 and/or Division 26 Furnished by mechanical, installed by electrical (or vice versa) Who provides the input/output conduit, who programs it, who provides the disconnecting means


Motor Starter Division 26 or in MCC schedule Included in motor control center by electrical Factory-mounted starters on equipment already in the mechanical quote


Disconnect Switch Division 26 or on electrical drawings Provided and installed by electrical Whether mechanical sub is expected to coordinate location, or who provides the feeder from the panel


Control Wiring Division 23 or 25 Low-voltage controls by mechanical or controls sub Who terminates at the VFD, who terminates at the BAS panel


The spec tells you what the designer intended. It does not tell you what the subs included in their number. Those are two different things.


## How the Gap Gets Locked In


It starts at bid day. The electrical sub scopes the project, sees the VFD called out in Division 23, and excludes it. The mechanical sub sees "VFD by electrical" in a note on the mechanical drawings, and excludes it too. Both exclusions are buried in clarification lists.


The GC receives bid packages, compares numbers, and selects the low trades. Nobody reconciles the exclusion language against the spec. The scope letters go out with generic language like "per plans and specifications" and both trades sign.


As one Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC described it: "If you miss anything, they'll bill it." That quote applies directly here. By the time the VFD question surfaces in the field, the GC owns the dispute.


This is one of the anti-patterns documented in[The Scope Gap Playbook's trade-specific chapter](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) : "as per plans and specs" is the most-cited anti-pattern in GC scope practice, precisely because it passes ambiguity downstream without resolving it.


## The Data Center and Healthcare Problem


This gap is not new. But it is getting bigger.


Data center specs run 1,500 to 2,500 pages. Healthcare projects carry dense Division 23/26 interplay, particularly around medical gas compressors, chiller plants, and air handling units. The number of VFD-driven motors on a single project can run into the hundreds.


When spec density increases, the probability that something is assigned in one division and silently excluded in another goes up. Estimators reading a 2,200-page spec set over two or three days will not catch every cross-reference. That is not a performance problem. It is a volume problem.


The $300K lead-lined glass gap documented in The Scope Gap Playbook followed the same logic: a specialty item sat at a trade boundary, the GC absorbed it under "readily inferable" language, and nobody caught it at buyout. The dollar amount was not exceptional. The pattern was.


## How to Write the Scope Letter to Close This Gap


You cannot rely on the spec to resolve trade boundaries for you. That is the job of your scope letter.


Here is a framework for MEP boundary assignments. Use this as a starting point, then tailor it to what the spec actually says.


### Step 1: Assign Supply and Installation Separately


For every motor-driven piece of equipment, write out who furnishes the VFD or starter and who installs it. Do not combine them into one line. Combined lines create room for each trade to claim the other side.


### Step 2: Name the Disconnecting Means Explicitly


Specify which trade provides and installs the disconnect switch at each motor location. Reference the section or drawing that shows it. If the electrical drawings show it, it goes in the electrical scope letter with a section cite.


### Step 3: Confirm Factory-Mounted vs. Field-Mounted


Before the scope letter goes out, confirm with the mechanical sub whether their equipment quote includes factory-mounted starters or VFDs. Get it in writing. If the answer is yes, exclude it from the electrical scope letter and document the confirmation.


### Step 4: Assign Control Wiring Explicitly


Low-voltage control wiring is a consistent source of finger-pointing. Assign it by circuit type: who runs conduit from the BAS panel to the VFD, who terminates at both ends, and who is responsible for point-to-point verification.


### Step 5: Run a Pre-Issue Scope Review Checkpoint


Before scope letters go to the trades, review MEP sections side by side. Look for items that appear in both Division 23 and Division 26 without a named trade. This is Habit 8 from The Scope Gap Playbook: the pre-issue scope review checkpoint. It takes 90 minutes and prevents weeks of field disputes.


As an Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC noted: "We have fewer subs who just rely on a gentleman's agreement. They've become more quick to clarify that they're not including that one piece of scope." The subs are protecting themselves. The GC needs to keep pace.


## What Good Scope Language Looks Like


Compare these two approaches:


**Weak:** "Electrical sub to include all items per Division 26 plans and specifications."


**Strong:** "Electrical sub to include: (1) disconnect switch at each motor location per E-201, Specification Section 26 28 23; (2) field wiring from MCC to motor, including conduit and terminations; (3) programming of VFDs at AHU-1 through AHU-6 per Spec Section 26 29 23. VFDs are factory-mounted by mechanical sub on AHU-1 through AHU-4. VFDs for AHU-5 and AHU-6 are field-mounted by electrical sub. Confirm in writing."


That level of detail is what keeps a $60,000 scope gap from becoming a $200,000 change order. The $60.1 million average North America construction dispute value cited in Arcadis's 2024 Global Construction Disputes Report does not start with large ambiguities. It starts with language like "per plans and specs" on a disconnect switch.

## The Bottom Line


VFDs, motor starters, and disconnects are small-dollar line items on any individual sheet. Across a healthcare or data center project, they add up. And when both trades exclude them, the GC pays.


The fix is not complicated. Write specific scope language. Cite the section. Confirm factory vs. field. Run the cross-trade review before the letters go out.


The subs are already doing this. They are protecting their numbers on every bid. The GC's scope letter needs to keep pace.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Who is typically responsible for providing VFDs on a commercial project?


It depends on the spec. Division 23 often assigns VFDs to the mechanical sub as part of HVAC equipment. Division 26 sometimes assigns them to electrical. The critical issue is confirming whether VFDs are factory-mounted in the equipment package or field-supplied separately. Write it down in the scope letter either way.


### What is the most common motor starter scope gap on ICI projects?


The most common gap is a factory-mounted starter included in the mechanical sub's equipment quote that the electrical sub also prices as a standalone item, or the reverse: both subs exclude it assuming the other owns it. Confirm factory vs. field-mounted status before scope letters go out.


### How should a GC assign disconnect switches in a scope letter?


Name the trade, cite the drawing or spec section, and specify location. For example: "Disconnect switch at each motor location per Drawing E-201 and Specification Section 26 28 23, furnished and installed by electrical sub." Generic language like "per plans and specs" leaves the assignment unresolved.


### Why are these gaps worse on data center and healthcare projects?


Spec density. Data center and healthcare specs routinely run 1,500 to 2,500 pages. Division 23 and Division 26 interplay is dense, and the number of motor-driven pieces of equipment is high. Estimators reading under time pressure will miss cross-trade boundary items. The gap is a volume problem, not just a skill problem.


### What does "readily inferable" mean for a GC on MEP scope?


It means the GC may be required to provide something not explicitly shown or specified if a reasonable contractor would have inferred it was required. For VFDs and disconnects, this is a real risk. If the spec requires a code-compliant installation and the disconnect is code-required, a court may find it was "readily inferable" even if no trade included it.


### Can AI tools reliably catch VFD and motor starter scope gaps in a spec set?


Purpose-built tools can. Generic AI tools lack the construction context to read Division 23 and Division 26 together and identify cross-trade boundary conflicts. Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) reads the full project set, including drawings and specs together, and flags these gaps with citations to the exact section and drawing reference.


### How do I find out if my subcontract exposes me on undefined MEP scope?


Review the "readily inferable," "work reasonably inferred," and "complete and proper execution" clauses in your subcontract. These are the most common mechanisms that shift undefined scope onto the GC.[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) identifies these clauses with 99% accuracy, cited to the exact location in the contract document.
